newsitem.title: USA: Steady Fed rates show Greenspan's realism -Blinder.
newsitem.headline: Steady Fed rates show Greenspan's realism -Blinder.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's decision on Tuesday to leave U.S. interest rates unchanged underscores that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan is a realist who puts facts above economic theories, said former Fed vice chairman Alan Blinder.

"Greenspan is not a doctrinaire person. He looks at the world as it is," added Blinder while referring to the unusual scenario of solid growth, low unemployment and declining inflation resulting in the healthiest U.S. economy in decades.

Blinder said Greenspan's focus on the surprisingly good inflation performance as well as his intuitive caution about economic doctrines were the main reasons accounting for the Fed's steady policy since March.

As widely expected, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on Tuesday left the federal funds rate unchanged at 5.50 percent, its level since it last tightened in March. That was the only tightening in more than two years and just the ninth rate hike in a six-year expansion -- the tamest tightening cycle since the 1970s.
The most challenging development for policymakers is that tight labor markets have not translated into wage pressures.

Such performance departs from traditional supply/demand theories such as the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment or NAIRU that estimates that a U.S. jobless rate below 5.75 percent would fuel wage-driven inflation.
The U.S. jobless rate has averaged 5.0 percent over the past six months, while inflation drifted to 2.5 percent -- its lowest since the mid-1960s.

"In order to make a case for a tightening (at this stage), you would have to be a strong believer in the NAIRU concept, with the NAIRU noticeably above 5.0 percent," said Blinder, who regularly discussed monetary policy with Greenspan during his tenure as Fed vice-chairman, from June 1994 to January 1996.

In his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony of February, Greenspan dismissed as "a mirage" the notion that structural changes resulted in a brave new economic world where rapid growth and declining prices coexisted.
But in his July testimony, Greenspan left the door open to the notion that changes, mainly in the area of productivity, may account for the American economic dream.
"The NAIRU has to be lower than it was believed to be," admitted Blinder, who now holds the chair of economics at Princeton University.

"We got some surprisingly, though not stunningly, good inflation performance. But the favorable inflation surprise is, so far, about a one standard deviation event," Blinder said of the temporary departure from the norm in a series.

Among the developments cited for the exceptionally good inflation performance, analysts have listed aggressive restructuring and job insecurity, the ageing of the U.S. workforce, massive business investments, new technology, productivity gains and international competition.

"The shift in demographics may explain the lower NAIRU a little bit, but it does not explain the whole thing. Another little bit of the good inflation story may come from globalization," Blinder admitted. "I'm still not sure that there are big fundamental changes. Rather, it looks like a lot of incremental things all pointing in the right direction."
